the cause, measured, and how I fix it

I measured both of your ideas against your real data. The one you picked is the better of the two — it keeps every piece small, and editing one task only rewrites that branch instead of the whole planner.

What changes. Each of your eight branches gets stored on its own, carrying its tasks, dates and repeats. Every note is stored separately again, and so is every journal day. Adding branches, notes or journal entries adds pieces rather than filling one, so the ceiling you are heading for stops existing.

You caught the journal and you were right. I had written this card around branches and task notes only. The journal is the same shape as a note — somewhere you write freely, one entry per day, growing forever. Leaving it in the main record would have moved the ceiling rather than removed it. Measured on your data, so nothing else is missed:

what you write intogets its own record?
a branch and its tasksyes — one per branch
a note inside a taskyes — one per note
a journal dayyes — one per day
deleted itemsno — stays in the main record, and emptying it frees the space
areas, habits, focus blocks, listsno — all tiny and fixed in size
now   → everything in one piece, 75% full
after → a piece per branch, a piece per note — none of them close to full

What you would notice: nothing. Same planner, same screens, same notes. A note loads when you open its task rather than everything loading at once, which on a large planner is faster.

And the pen mark keeps working — you were right to ask. A task with notes shows a small amber ✎ on its row. That is not cosmetic: it is how you tell, at a glance, that there is writing inside something without opening it.

Here is exactly how the split could have broken it, which is worth saying because it would have broken silently:

the pen asks the task  → “do you have notes?”
after the split      → the notes live elsewhere, so the task says no
result: every pen disappears, and nothing warns you

So each task keeps a marker saying “there is a note here” even once the writing itself has moved out. The pen reads that, and looks exactly as it does now. Measured in your build: 11 places draw this pen — the tree, Completed, Deleted and Past due — and all of them ask the same single function, so fixing it once fixes all four.

The check proves it the hard way: every task that shows a pen today must still show one afterwards, counted on screen, not assumed.

One thing worth telling you. Your note "App update ideas" is far larger than every other note you have — big enough that it would eventually fill a piece on its own, though not for a long while. When that matters the answer is to split that one note behind the scenes. I am naming it now rather than letting it surprise you later.

The popup instead of a gauge. You were right that no ordinary app shows a fullness meter. Nothing appears anywhere until you pass 80%, and then it is a single popup when you sign in — what the number is, what happens if it fills, and a button to clear the quickest thing out.

Three things before you approve.

  • This is the riskiest change we have discussed. It changes how every screen loads and saves. You are at 75% with 256 KB spare, so there is room to do it carefully rather than quickly. I would ship the Settings menu and the backups first, and come back to this.
  • A check has to prove nothing was lost. Every task, every note and every journal day, read back character for character after the split and compared against what it was before. Not a count, not a sample — all of them. If one does not match, it does not ship. The check also walks the whole of your data and fails if it finds any writing surface the split did not account for, so a future one cannot be forgotten the way the journal nearly was.
  • The pen mark gets its own check, because it would fail quietly. Nothing errors if the pens stop appearing — your tasks just look like they have nothing written in them. So the check counts the pens on screen before the split and after, on all four lists that draw them, and the numbers have to match. That is the kind of defect I would otherwise only find when you told me about it.
  • The popup needs a rule about not nagging. Shown at sign-in past 80% is what you asked for; if you dismiss it I would not show it again that day. Say if you want it every sign-in regardless.

the cause, measured, and how I fix it

Nothing is built. This is not in your planner and not in the copy planner. You asked me to park it — “don’t do anything on it yet… its just to remind me to do it later when this copy planner is done” — so this card is a reminder, nothing more.

I did measure the cause, so that when you do say go, the card starts from a fact rather than a guess. I ran your planner’s own describing code over thirteen kinds of change:

what you dowhat the Undo row says
change a task’s durationCall the accountant — duration 60 min → 90 min
rename a taskRenamed Call the accountant → Call the bookkeeper
delete or add a tasknames it
tick a task offdone empty → yes
move a taskChanged a task
rename an areaChanged a task
tally a habitChanged a task
write in the journalChanged a task
edit a noteChanged a task
add to a listChanged a task

Seven of thirteen come out useless — and the first of them is moving a task, which is probably what your four rows were, since they arrived within a minute of each other.

Why. Your planner already has a describer, and it is good at tasks — it was built in September for this same complaint. But it only ever looks at the task tree, while an Undo entry is recorded for every save. So a change anywhere else — areas, habits, the journal, notes, lists — has nothing to describe it and falls back to that one sentence. A move falls through too, because moving a task changes none of its fields, only its place.

What I would do when you say go: teach the existing describer the other five places and teach it about position, so a move reads “Moved Call the accountant under Work”. Not a second history — the one you have is fine, it just cannot see most of your planner.
